q: You want to start learning to drive a car. What's the youngest age at which you can apply for a provisional driving licence?
explain: You can apply for a provisional driving licence when you're 15 years and 9 months old. You can usually start driving a car when you're 17.

q: A friend has offered to supervise you while you practise driving. What are the minimum requirements they must meet?
options: Aged 18 or over, and held a full licence for 1 year
Aged 21 or over, and held a full licence for 1 year
Aged 21 or over, and held a full licence for 3 years
Aged 18 or over, and held a full licence for 3 years
explain: Learners MUST be supervised by someone at least 21 years old who holds a full licence for that type of car (automatic or manual) and has held one for at least 3 years.

q: Your mother has held a full licence for automatic cars only for 10 years. Can she supervise you while you learn in a manual car?
options: No, she needs a manual car licence
Yes, as long as she's over 21
Yes, as she's held her licence for over 3 years
Yes, if the car has dual controls
explain: Anyone supervising you must be qualified to drive the type of vehicle you're learning in. For example, they must have a manual car licence if they're supervising you in a manual car.

q: You're supervising a learner driver. Which of these would be illegal for you to do?
options: Sit in the front passenger seat
explain: You MUST NOT use a hand-held mobile phone or similar device when driving or when supervising a learner driver.

q: Your family car has L plates on it for your son, who is learning. You're driving it on your own. What should you do with the plates?
options: Move them to the back only
explain: L plates should be removed or covered when the vehicle isn't being driven by a learner (except on driving school vehicles).

q: You're learning to drive in your family's car. Where must the L plates be displayed?
explain: You must put an L plate on the front and back of your vehicle so they can be seen easily. L plates must have a red L on a white background and be the right size. In Wales, you can use a D plate instead.

q: A learner driver is caught driving without the right supervision. What's the maximum number of penalty points they could get on their provisional licence?
explain: You can be fined up to £1,000 and get up to 6 penalty points on your provisional licence if you drive without the right supervision.

q: What must you have before you can book your car theory test?
explain: You must have a provisional driving licence to book your theory test. There's no minimum number of lessons you must have.

q: You've just passed your theory test. How long is your pass certificate number valid for?
explain: Your theory test pass certificate number lasts for 2 years. You must pass your driving test in that time, otherwise you'll have to pass the theory test again.

q: What's the minimum type of motor insurance you must have by law?
explain: Third-party insurance is the minimum cover required by law. It covers anyone you might injure or whose property you might damage.

q: Your car is insured for third party only. You lose control and hit a neighbour's garden wall, damaging both the wall and your car. What will your insurance cover?
options: Damage to your own car only
Damage to both the wall and your car
Nothing, as no other vehicle was involved
explain: Third-party insurance covers anyone you might injure or whose property you might damage. It doesn't cover damage to your own vehicle or injury to yourself.

q: Which type of insurance would cover damage to your own car, up to its market value, after a collision that was your fault?
explain: Comprehensive insurance is the most expensive but the best cover. As well as covering other people and property, it covers damage to your own vehicle, up to its market value, and personal injury to yourself.

q: The police catch you driving a car that you're not insured to drive. What fixed penalty could they give you?
explain: The police could give you a fixed penalty of £300 and 6 penalty points for driving a vehicle you're not insured to drive. If the case goes to court you could get an unlimited fine and be disqualified, and the police can seize the vehicle.

q: A police officer asks to see your driving documents, but you don't have them with you. Within how many days may you be asked to take them to a police station?
explain: You MUST be able to produce your driving licence, a valid insurance certificate and (if appropriate) a valid MOT certificate when asked by a police officer. If you can't, you may be asked to take them to a police station within 7 days.

q: A police officer stops you and asks to see your documents. Which of these could they ask you to produce?
explain: If a police officer asks, you must be able to show your driving licence, a valid insurance certificate and a valid MOT certificate (if your vehicle needs one).

q: You've bought a brand-new car for private use. By when must it have its first MOT?
options: The first anniversary of its registration
The second anniversary of its registration
The third anniversary of its registration
The fifth anniversary of its registration
explain: You must get an MOT for your car by the third anniversary of its registration, and then by the anniversary of its last MOT.

q: Your car is 5 years old. How often must it have an MOT?
explain: Cars must normally pass an MOT test 3 years from the date of first registration and every year after that. An MOT lasts for a year.

q: Your car's MOT certificate has run out. When may you drive it on the road?
options: At any time, as long as it's taxed
To a pre-arranged MOT test appointment
For up to 7 days after it runs out
To work, if you've booked a test
explain: You can't drive your vehicle on the road if the MOT has run out. The only exceptions are driving it to or from somewhere to be repaired, or to a pre-arranged MOT test. You can be fined up to £1,000 for driving without a valid MOT.

q: Your car's MOT has expired and its vehicle tax is due to run out. What does this mean?
options: You can tax it now and book an MOT later
Your tax will be extended automatically
You'll get a 14-day grace period for both
You can't renew the tax until it has a valid MOT
explain: You can't renew your vehicle tax if your MOT has expired. If your tax is due to run out, register the vehicle as off the road (SORN), book an MOT and tax the vehicle once it has passed.

q: Your car is exempt from vehicle tax, so there's nothing to pay. What must you still do?
explain: You must tax your vehicle even if you don't have to pay anything because it's exempt from vehicle tax.

q: You're keeping a car in your garage and won't be taxing or insuring it. What must you do?
options: Send the log book back to DVLA
explain: If you're the keeper and want to keep a vehicle untaxed and off the public road, you MUST make a Statutory Off Road Notification (SORN). It's an offence not to, and the vehicle stays SORN until you tax, sell or scrap it.

q: You've made a SORN for your car. When may you drive it on a public road?
options: For short journeys of under 5 miles
explain: You can only drive a vehicle with a SORN on a public road to go to or from a pre-booked MOT or other testing appointment. Using it for any other reason could lead to prosecution and a fine of up to £2,500.

q: You made a SORN for your car last year. You now want to start using it on the road again. What must you do?
options: Wait for the SORN to expire
explain: A SORN is cancelled automatically when you tax your vehicle again, and you don't need to renew it. You must insure and tax a vehicle that doesn't have a SORN, and it must have a current MOT if it needs one.

q: You've sold your car privately. Who is responsible for sending the completed registration certificate (V5C) to DVLA?
explain: You MUST tell DVLA as soon as possible when you buy or sell a vehicle. The buyer and seller complete the registration certificate, and the seller is responsible for sending it to DVLA.

q: What information does a vehicle registration certificate (V5C) give?
options: Proof that the car is roadworthy
Proof that the car is insured
explain: Registration certificates are issued for all motor vehicles used on the road. They describe the vehicle (make, model, etc) and give details of the registered keeper.

q: You've just moved house. What must you do about your driving licence?
options: Nothing until your licence needs renewing
Apply for a new provisional licence
explain: You MUST tell DVLA if you change your address. It doesn't cost anything, and you can be fined up to £1,000 if you don't. You must also change the address on your vehicle log book (V5C).

q: You passed your driving test 18 months ago. How many penalty points would lead to your licence being revoked?
explain: Under the New Drivers Act, your licence will be revoked if you get 6 or more penalty points within 2 years of passing your first driving test. This applies even if you pay for offences by fixed penalty.

q: A new driver's licence has been revoked under the New Drivers Act. What must they do to get a full licence again?
options: Pass both the theory and practical tests again
Retake only the practical driving test
explain: If your licence is revoked within 2 years of passing, you'll have to apply and pay for a new provisional licence and pass both the theory and practical tests again to get a full licence.

q: You got 3 penalty points while you were a learner driver. You've now passed your test. What happens to those points?
options: They're wiped when you pass your test
They're doubled on your full licence
They're carried over to your full licence
They only count if you fail a test
explain: Any penalty points on your provisional licence that haven't expired are carried over to your full licence. If further points take you to a total of 6 or more within 2 years of passing, your licence will be revoked.

q: A driver who passed their test many years ago keeps getting penalty points. Under the 'totting-up' rules, how many points within 3 years mean they MUST be disqualified?
explain: A driver who builds up 12 or more penalty points within 3 years MUST be disqualified. This will be for a minimum of 6 months, or longer if they've been disqualified before.

q: A driver is convicted of driving with alcohol above the legal limit (code DR10). How long must the endorsement stay on their driving record?
options: 4 years from the date of the offence
11 years from the date of conviction
3 years from the date of conviction
5 years from the date of the offence
explain: Endorsements stay on your driving record for 4 or 11 years, depending on the offence. Drink-driving endorsements (codes DR10 to DR61) must stay on your record for 11 years from the date of conviction.

q: You get penalty points for exceeding the speed limit on a public road (code SP30). How long must the endorsement stay on your driving record?
options: 4 years from the date of the offence
11 years from the date of conviction
2 years from the date of the offence
5 years from the date of conviction
explain: Speed limit endorsements (SP10 to SP50) must stay on your driving record for 4 years from the date of the offence.

q: You've developed a health condition that's likely to affect your driving. What MUST you do?
options: Display a medical notice in your car
explain: You MUST report to DVLA any health condition likely to affect your driving.

q: Which of these eyesight problems must you tell DVLA about?
explain: You must tell DVLA if you've got any problem with your eyesight that affects both of your eyes, or the remaining eye if you only have one eye. This doesn't include being short-sighted, long-sighted or colour blind.

q: You need to wear glasses to read a number plate from 20 metres away. When MUST you wear them?
explain: You MUST be able to read a vehicle number plate, in good daylight, from 20 metres. If you need glasses or contact lenses to do this, you MUST wear them every time you drive.
